story: Manu is the archetypal first man and progenitor of humanity. In later tradition, Manu becomes the title of fourteen successive rulers, each heading a great age (manvantara) within a cosmic cycle; when one age ends, a new Manu begins the next. The first Manu, Svayambhuva, was born from the mind of the creator god Brahma and married to Shatarupa. Their daughters married sages and gods, producing many divine and human lines, and two of their grandsons were incarnations of the god Vishnu. Svayambhuva and his wife practiced austerities in a forest by a river until demon-like Rakshasas attacked them; his grandson Yajna, aided by minor gods, killed the attackers and then took the throne of the king of heaven, Indra. Each subsequent Manu had his own sons, sages, and guardian deities, and Vishnu appeared in a different incarnation during each age to protect the world. The seventh Manu, Vaivasvata, ruled a kingdom before a great flood. The fish-avatar of Vishnu warned him of the coming deluge and instructed him to build a boat. Manu loaded the boat with sacred scriptures, his own family, and seven sages, and the fish towed the boat to safety, preserving humanity and knowledge through the flood. This tale of warning, boat-building, and rescue is repeated with variations in other sacred texts. Later Manus continued the pattern: each had sons who became kings, each age had its own Indra and seven sages, and each was watched over by a fresh incarnation of Vishnu, some of whom performed heroic deeds such as slaying demons or liberating devotees, until the fourteenth and final Manu of the current cosmic cycle.
